units.title: 3.1 The operation of markets and market failure

topics.title: 3.1.1 Economic methodology and the economic problem

outcomes.text: Know what the study of markets and market failure covers.
Understand economic methodology and the economic problem.
Describe economics as a social science and compare its methods with the natural sciences.
Distinguish positive from normative statements.
Explain how value judgements, and moral and political views, influence decisions and policy.
Explain that economic activity produces goods and services to meet needs and wants.
State the key decisions: what, how and for whom to produce.
Classify resources as land, labour, capital and enterprise.
Explain that the environment is a scarce resource.
Explain scarcity as limited resources against unlimited wants.
Explain that scarcity forces choices about allocating resources.
Explain opportunity cost.
Use production possibility diagrams to show allocation, opportunity cost, trade-offs, unemployed resources and growth.
Explain why every boundary point is productively efficient but not necessarily allocatively efficient.

topics.title: 3.1.2 Price determination in a competitive market

outcomes.text: Understand how prices are set in a competitive market.
Explain the factors determining demand for a good or service.
Explain the demand curve as the price-quantity demanded relationship.
Explain the causes of shifts in demand, including income, wealth, related goods and preferences.
Calculate price, income and cross elasticities of demand and interpret the values.
Relate income elasticity to normal and inferior goods, and cross elasticity to substitutes and complements.
Relate price elasticity of demand to total revenue.
Explain the factors influencing these elasticities.
Explain the factors determining supply.
Explain the supply curve and how higher prices give an incentive to expand production.
Explain the causes of shifts in supply.
Calculate price elasticity of supply and interpret the value.
Explain the factors influencing it.
Explain how demand and supply set equilibrium prices.
Distinguish equilibrium from disequilibrium.
Explain how excess demand or supply changes price, using diagrams on real markets.
Explain how changes in one market affect others.
Explain joint demand, substitutes, composite demand, derived demand and joint supply.
Understand production, costs and revenue.
Explain how production turns inputs into output.
Define productivity, including labour productivity.
Explain the benefits of specialisation and division of labour.
Explain why specialisation needs an efficient means of exchange such as money.
Distinguish the short run from the long run.
Distinguish fixed from variable costs and average from total costs.
Calculate average and total costs from data.
Explain the shape of short-run and long-run average cost curves.
Distinguish internal from external economies of scale and give examples.
Explain reasons for diseconomies of scale.
Relate scale effects to the long-run average cost curve.
Distinguish average from total revenue.
Explain why average revenue is the firm's demand curve.
Define profit as total revenue minus total costs and calculate it.
Understand competitive and concentrated markets.
Explain that market structures differ in number of firms, product differentiation and ease of entry.
Explain profit as a main objective and other aims such as survival, growth and market share.
Explain that objectives affect firm behaviour.
Describe the characteristics of a perfectly competitive market, with price set by demand and supply.
Explain why profits are likely lower in competitive markets than in markets dominated by few firms.
Distinguish pure monopoly from monopoly power.
Explain factors influencing monopoly power: barriers, competitors, advertising, differentiation.
Calculate and use concentration ratios.
Explain how monopoly can raise prices, profits and inefficiency, misallocating resources.
Explain potential monopoly benefits such as economies of scale and innovation.
Explain that firms compete on improved products, lower costs and service quality as well as price.
Recognise that monopoly power may exploit consumers.

topics.title: 3.1.5 The market mechanism, market failure and government intervention in markets

outcomes.text: Understand markets, market failure and intervention.
Explain the rationing, incentive and signalling functions of prices.
Explain the price mechanism as the way a market economy resolves the economic problem.
Define market failure as misallocation of resources.
Distinguish complete (missing market) from partial market failure.
Explain how public goods, externalities, merit and demerit goods, monopoly and inequality cause market failure.
Describe pure public goods as non-rival and non-excludable.
Distinguish public from private goods and explain quasi-public goods.
Explain how technology changes excludability.
Explain the free-rider problem.
Define externalities as divergence between private and social costs and benefits.
Explain why negative externalities cause over-production and positive ones under-production.
Illustrate misallocation from externalities on demand and supply diagrams.
Explain that merit and demerit classification rests on value judgements.
Explain consumption externalities of such goods.
Explain how imperfect information causes under-provision of merit goods and over-provision of demerit goods.
Recognise that not every product with consumption externalities is merit or demerit.
Explain how imperfect and asymmetric information causes market failure.
Explain how monopoly power causes market failure.
Explain how immobility of factors of production causes market failure.
Explain why markets tend to produce unequal, inequitable income and wealth.
Explain why such inequality can misallocate resources.
Know that progressive taxes and government spending reduce inequality.
Explain market failure as an argument for intervention.
Describe how government affects resource allocation through spending, taxation and regulation.
Explain how government objectives shape intervention.
Explain indirect taxes, subsidies, price controls, state provision and regulation.
Evaluate the case for and against intervention and compare methods.
Define government failure as intervention that misallocates resources.
Explain sources: inadequate information, conflicting objectives, administrative costs.
Explain how governments can create distortions and unintended consequences.

units.title: 3.2 The national economy in a global context

outcomes.text: Know what the study of the national economy in a global context covers.
Understand how macroeconomic performance is measured.
State the main objectives: growth, price stability, low unemployment and a stable current account.
Explain possible short-run conflicts between objectives and that their priority changes over time.
Use real GDP, real GDP per capita, CPI/RPI, unemployment, productivity and the current account to measure performance.
Calculate and interpret index numbers, including base year and weights.
Use index numbers to measure changes in the price level and other variables, knowing the 'basket of goods' idea.

topics.title: 3.2.2 How the macroeconomy works: the circular flow of income, aggregate demand/aggregate supply analysis, and related concepts

outcomes.text: Understand how the macroeconomy works.
Explain what national income measures and distinguish nominal from real income.
Explain the circular flow, income = output = expenditure, equilibrium and full employment income.
Distinguish injections from withdrawals and explain their effect on national income.
Explain price level changes as movements along AD and AS curves.
Explain factors shifting AD and short-run AS, and those affecting long-run AS.
Show underlying growth as a rightward shift of long-run AS.
Use AD/AS diagrams for equilibrium, demand-side and supply-side shocks, price level changes, cyclical unemployment and growth.
Define AD and explain determinants: consumption, investment, government spending, exports and imports.
Explain the basic accelerator.
Explain the determinants of saving and distinguish saving from investment.
Explain AD's role in the level of economic activity.
Explain the multiplier and calculate it from a change in injections and resulting national income.
Explain that the price level and production costs determine short-run AS.
Explain how wage, raw material, business tax and productivity changes shift it.
Explain long-run AS determinants: technology, productivity, attitudes, enterprise, factor mobility, incentives.
Explain the vertical long-run AS curve as normal capacity output.
Understand how an economy performs.
Distinguish short-run from long-run growth and explain their demand-side and supply-side determinants.
Use PPC and AD/AS diagrams to illustrate the difference.
Explain the economic cycle and identify its phases from indicators.
Distinguish positive from negative output gaps.
Explain demand-side and supply-side shocks, including global ones.
Describe the UK claimant count and Labour Force Survey measures.
Distinguish seasonal, frictional, structural and cyclical unemployment.
Explain demand-side and supply-side determinants and the effect of the world economy.
Explain that policies to cut unemployment depend on its cause.
Explain inflation, deflation and disinflation.
Explain demand-pull and cost-push inflation.
Explain how world commodity prices and other economies affect UK inflation.
Explain the importance of international trade to an economy such as the UK.
Describe the current account: goods, services, primary and secondary income.
Explain deficit and surplus.
Explain factors affecting the balance: productivity, inflation, exchange rate and foreign activity.
Relate output gaps to unemployment and inflationary pressure.
Explain how policies may reconcile conflicts in the short and long run, using AD/AS.
Understand macroeconomic policy.
Describe monetary policy: interest rates, money and credit supply, exchange rate.
Describe current monetary policy objectives and the MPC's use of bank rate to target inflation.
Explain the factors the MPC considers.
Explain how exchange rate changes affect AD and policy objectives.
Describe fiscal policy: government spending, taxation and the budget balance.
Explain macroeconomic and microeconomic functions, and effects on AD, AS and activity patterns.
Distinguish direct from indirect taxes and progressive, proportional and regressive taxes.
Explain the link between budget balance and national debt, and know main UK taxes and spending.
Distinguish supply-side policies from supply-side improvements.
Explain how policies such as tax-incentive changes raise potential output and trend growth.
Explain effects on unemployment, price change and the current account.
Describe measures: education and training spending, tax cuts, welfare reform, industrial policy.

subtopics.title: Diminishing returns and returns to scale

outcomes.text: Distinguish the short run from the long run.
Distinguish marginal, average and total returns.
Explain the law of diminishing returns.
Explain increasing, constant and decreasing returns to scale and their cost implications.
Distinguish fixed from variable costs and marginal, average and total costs.
Distinguish short-run from long-run costs.
Calculate costs from data and draw and interpret cost curves, explaining their shapes.
Explain how factor prices and productivity affect costs and input choice.
Distinguish internal from external economies of scale and give examples.
Explain reasons for diseconomies of scale.
Relate returns to scale to economies and diseconomies and to the long-run average cost curve.

topics.title: 4.1.5 Perfect competition, imperfectly competitive markets and monopoly

outcomes.text: Understand market structures from perfect competition to monopoly.
Describe the competition spectrum from perfect competition to pure monopoly.
Distinguish structures by number of firms, product differentiation and ease of entry.
Explain that traditional theory assumes profit maximisation, with the MC = MR rule.
Explain the reasons and consequences of separation of ownership from control.
Describe other objectives: survival, growth, quality, sales revenue and market share.
Explain the satisficing principle.
Analyse perfect competition by diagram in the short and long run.
Explain implications of many producers, identical products, free entry and exit, and perfect knowledge.
Explain that firms are price takers.
Assess whether perfect competition yields efficient allocation, and use it as a yardstick.
Analyse monopolistic competition by diagram in the short and long run.
Describe its main characteristics and non-price competition.
Describe oligopoly characteristics and how it can be defined by structure or by conduct.
Calculate and use concentration ratios.
Distinguish collusive from non-collusive oligopoly and cooperation from collusion.
Use the kinked demand curve to illustrate interdependence.
Explain non-price competition, cartels, price leadership, price agreements, price wars and entry barriers.
Explain factors affecting prices, output, investment, R&D and advertising, and the role of interdependence and uncertainty.
Evaluate advantages and disadvantages of oligopoly.
Analyse monopoly by diagram.
Explain factors influencing monopoly power: barriers, competitors, advertising, differentiation.
Evaluate advantages and disadvantages of monopoly, and recognise monopoly power in other structures.
Explain the conditions needed for price discrimination.
Analyse price discrimination by diagram and assess advantages and disadvantages for producers and consumers.
Explain short-run and long-run benefits of competition.
Explain that firms compete on products, costs and service as well as price.
Explain creative destruction and entry that erodes monopoly profit.
Explain the significance of market contestability for industry performance.
Explain sunk costs and hit-and-run competition.
Distinguish static from dynamic efficiency.
Explain productive efficiency (minimum average total cost) and allocative efficiency (price = marginal cost).
Explain influences on dynamic efficiency: R&D, investment, technology.
Compare firm performance in different market structures using conduct and performance indicators.
Explain consumer and producer surplus by diagram.
Apply them to efficiency and welfare issues such as price discrimination and monopoly deadweight loss.
Understand how labour markets work.
Explain that labour demand is derived from product demand.
Explain marginal productivity theory of labour demand.
Explain the labour demand curve and its shifts.
Explain the determinants of the elasticity of demand for labour.
Explain how monetary and non-monetary factors influence labour supply to an occupation.
Explain the labour supply curve and its shifts.
Explain the wage model in a perfectly competitive labour market.
Explain how market forces set relative wages.
Explain how monopsony, trade unions and imperfect information create labour market imperfections.
Show how a monopsonist cuts wage and employment below the competitive level, using diagrams.
Explain factors affecting unions' ability to influence wages and employment.
Show how a union affects wages and employment in a competitive and a monopsony market.
Explain effects of a national minimum wage on labour markets.
Evaluate its advantages and disadvantages.
Explain the conditions necessary for wage discrimination.
Explain the effect of gender, ethnicity and other discrimination on wages, employment levels and types.
Assess pros and cons of wage discrimination for workers, employers and the economy.

topics.title: 4.1.7 The distribution of income and wealth: poverty and inequality

outcomes.text: Understand inequality and poverty.
Distinguish income from wealth and explain what influences their distribution.
Distinguish equality from equity.
Interpret the Lorenz curve and Gini coefficient.
Evaluate benefits and costs of more equal and more unequal distributions.
Distinguish relative from absolute poverty.
Explain the causes and effects of poverty.
Describe policies to influence distribution and reduce poverty.
Evaluate their economic consequences and the moral and political views involved.
